text:
Haud putaverim, ita hæc sensa Deiparæ a S. Sophronio tribui quasi persuasum reipsa sancto doctori fuerit, tunc sanctam Virginem hæc elocutam fuisse. Citius dixerim, more eorum, qui ex Gr. laudibus celebrantes sancti Præcursoris nativitatem, hunc utut in utero matris adhuc inclusum anticipatione quadam inducunt sublimia quæque de divinis disserentem, sic sanctum Sophronium ista de sancta Dei Genitrice pro sensis potius, quæ fidelibus inesse de eadem noverat, quam pro rei gestæ verisimilitudine protulisse, atque eadem plane de causa factum cernis, ut Gabrielis archangeli ad Virginem alloquiis illa Sophronius intermisceat, quæ ad refutandas hæreses Nestorii et Eutychetis adversus incarnationis Dominicæ mysterium opportuna videbantur, licet ea ab angelo tunc dicta fuisse, nemo sibi persuadeat.
Cæterum haud levis momenti fuerit, apud christianam plebem exploratissima tunc ea fuisse, quæ in hac Sophronii oratione legimus. Concludi enim inde potest, vulgatissimam ergo in Ecclesia doctrinam exstitisse, quæ tradit, eum locum in divina regenerationis humanæ œconomia tribuendum esse Deiparæ, qui in prima olim humani generis conditione veteri illi Evæ datus fuerat, adeo ut quæcunque primæ hujus matris propria fuerunt, ad sanctam Dei Genitricem transferenda sint. Et sane, nonne ex his Sophronii verbis patet, comparationem Mariæ inter et Evam eo usque perductam fuisse, ut sanctæ Virginis deceptio (si qua locum habuisset), et lapsus nonnisi primæ matris deceptioni et lapsui æquiparanda forent, neque minus ab illius quam hujus gestis aut rectis aut pravis universi humani generis seu sospitas seu pernicies penderet ?
Sed et ulterius aliquid ex his elucet, quod pressius ad rem præsentem spectat, nempe ex recepta tunc doctrina non aliam, ac Evæ fuerit ante lapsum, Mariæ conditionem exstitisse. Propterea hypotheticam illam sanctæ Virginis deceptionem non cum ulla ex omnigenis prævaricationibus eorum, qui in statu naturæ lapsæ versantur, sed cum Evæ errore conferri hic cernis. Propterea Virgo se comparat Evæ (sup. § 23), cum ad hanc serpens primo accessit, et quam idcirco (§ præs. paulo inf.) diserte dicit adhuc malitiæ expertem. Propterea angelus (§ 24 et 25) cum plura verset, quo testetur se non eum esse, qui in errorem ac perniciem impellat, nullas insidias memorat ac nullas ruinas, nisi quæ ad protoparentum lapsum pertinent. Huc et illud spectat, quod ejusmodi fingitur deceptio, quæ, non secus ac Evæ factum est, a divina charitate (§ 23) dejiciat : nam hæc utique idoneum sensum habent, si sanctam Virginem eo loci constitutam reputes, quem tenuit Eva ante peccatum ; contra vero nonne carent omni sensu, si Mariam quoque lapsis hominibus accenseas ? Orationis enim series non aliter lapsos homines exhibet aut exhibere hic potest (vid. a § 12 ad 18) quam peccati tenebris et umbra mortis involutos, quibus idcirco restauratio per incarnationis opus divinitus paratur ; nullus ergo locus superest divinæ gratiæ luci, e qua Maria excidere possit, siquidem ipsam quoque inter lapsos connumeres. Huc denique collineat, quod graviores adhuc ruinæ universo humano generi ex hypothetica Mariæ ruina impendere perhibeatur (§ præs.) : nunquid enim hæc palam non faciunt, ex recepta tunc doctrina veteri Evæ sic Mariam fuisse substitutam, ut, non secus atque illa, novi ordinis principium foret, novumque denuo quoddam periculum ac veluti certamen in ipsa instauraretur, cujus exitus novæ aut felicitatis aut infelicitatis origo humano generi exsisteret ? Hinc est, quod et sanctus Proclus (homilia 6, § 16) dæmones non modo consilia de sancta Virgine expugnanda tanquam de summa rerum agitantes, sed etiam expresse tanquam cum secunda Eva, æque ac prior illa, adhuc innocenti et integra bellum parantes inducat : At iterumne (inquit) cum secunda Eva nobis instat certamen ? Instruendane acies adversus impollutam mulierem ? ..... Quonam itaque modo naviculam ejusmodi tempestate jactabimus ? ..... Quonam modo discerpemus ovem ? ..... Quonam modo diripiemus civitatem ? Ἀλλὰ πάλιν ἡμῖν ἐστι πρὸς δευτέραν ὁ πόλεμος, πρὸς ἄφθορον γυναῖκα ἡ παράταξις ; Quo in loco ut vim earum vocum ἄφθορον γυναῖκα plene percipias, adverte, quod contra Proclus subdidit de priori Eva : Ἐκείνη τῆς φθορᾶς μεταλαβοῦσα, τῆς ὑπερκειμένης ἀξίας λαβέσθαι διενοεῖτο· Illa cum corruptionem sibi assumeret, eminentem dignitatem capessere se existimabat ; Ἄφθορον ergo Proclus Mariam dicit, utpote ab illa cor-
anchorLine: viorumque calamitatum auctrix evadam (33).
en: I would hardly suppose that these sentiments of the Mother of God are attributed to St. Sophronius as though the holy doctor had been actually persuaded that the holy Virgin spoke these words. I would rather say that, after the manner of those who in Greek laudations celebrate the nativity of the holy Forerunner, introducing him, though still enclosed in his mother's womb, by a kind of anticipation as discoursing on lofty divine matters, so Sophronius put these things about the holy Mother of God into her mouth rather according to the sense of what he knew the faithful held of her than for the likelihood of the event; and for the very same reason you see him mix into the angel Gabriel's words to the Virgin things that seemed suited to refuting the heresies of Nestorius and Eutyches against the mystery of the Lord's incarnation, although let no one persuade himself that these were said by the angel at that time. [Next paragraph:] It is of no slight importance that what we read in this oration was then very well known among the Christian people. For it can be concluded from this that the doctrine was very widespread in the Church which holds that the place in the divine economy of human regeneration is to be assigned to the Mother of God which in the first condition of the human race was given to that former Eve, so that whatever things were proper to this first mother are to be transferred to the holy Mother of God. And indeed, is it not plain from these words of Sophronius that the comparison between Mary and Eve was carried so far that the deception of the holy Virgin (if it had had any place), and her fall, would be equated only with the deception and fall of the first mother, and that the safety or destruction of the whole human race would depend no less on her deeds, right or wrong, than on the other's? [Next paragraph:] But something further also shines out from these words, which bears more closely on the present matter: namely that, according to the doctrine then received, Mary's condition was no other than Eve's had been before the fall. Hence you see that the hypothetical deception of the holy Virgin is compared here not with any of the manifold transgressions of those who live in the state of fallen nature, but with Eve's error. Hence the Virgin compares herself to Eve (above, § 23) when the serpent first approached her, and whom for that reason (§ present, a little below) she expressly calls still ignorant of malice. Hence the angel (§§ 24 and 25), though he treats of many things by which he testifies that he is not one who drives her into error and ruin, mentions no snares and no ruins except those pertaining to the fall of the first parents. To this too belongs the point that a deception of such kind is imagined as, no less than in Eve's case, would cast her down from divine love (§ 23): for these words make fitting sense if you consider the holy Virgin placed in the position Eve held before sin; but on the contrary do they not lack all sense if you reckon Mary also among fallen men? For the course of the oration shows fallen men, or can here show them, only as wrapped in the darkness of sin and the shadow of death (see from § 12 to 18), for whom therefore restoration is divinely prepared through the work of the incarnation; there is therefore no place left of the light of divine grace from which Mary could fall, if you number her too among the fallen. Finally this points the same way, that graver ruins are said to threaten the whole human race from the hypothetical ruin of Mary (§ present): do not these things openly show that, by the received doctrine, Mary was thus substituted for the old Eve so that, no less than she, she should be the beginning of a new order, and a new danger and, as it were, contest should be set up anew in her, the outcome of which would become for the human race the source of new happiness or unhappiness? Hence it is that St. Proclus (homily 6, § 16) represents the demons not only as planning designs against the holy Virgin as if debating the sum of things, but expressly as preparing war against one who, like the first Eve, is still innocent and whole: 'Is there then again, with the second Eve, a contest upon us? Are battle lines to be drawn against an undefiled woman? ..... In what manner then shall we toss such a little boat with tempest? ..... In what manner shall we tear the sheep apart? ..... In what manner shall we plunder the city?' But [in Greek:] 'Again for us the war is against a second one, the battle line against an incorrupt woman.' Where, that you may fully grasp the force of the words 'incorrupt woman', note what Proclus added concerning the first Eve: 'She, having shared in corruption, thought to lay hold of the higher dignity'; [Latin:] 'She, taking corruption to herself, thought she was seizing an eminent dignity.' In confesso igitur esse debet, comparationem Mariam inter et Evam eo spectare, ut Maria-Evæ ante lapsum innocenti ceu nova ac nobilior Eva æquiparetur, quemadmodum novus Adam Christus veteri Adamo suffectus fuit. Quod utrumque Zeno Veronensis complectitur, cum divinam charitatem mundi restauratricem alloquens inquit (lib. 1, tract. II, n. 9, p. 25, Veron., 1739) : Tu Evam in Mariam redintegrasti : tu Adam in Christo renovasti. Sed de his plura in Commentario.
en: ...from corruption (φθορά) the corruption which the first Eve incurred by eating of the tree. It must therefore be granted that the comparison between Mary and Eve looks to this: that Mary-Eve, innocent before the fall, is equated with Eve as a new and nobler Eve, just as the new Adam, Christ, was put in the place of the old Adam. Zeno of Verona embraces both when, addressing divine charity as the restorer of the world, he says (book 1, tract. 2, n. 9, p. 25, Verona, 1739): 'You have restored Eve in Mary; you have renewed Adam in Christ.' But more on these things in the Commentary.

en: If the distinguished Cardinal Angelo Mai thought the testimony of Cosmas to be not negligible, as ancient, in favour of Anne as mother of the divine Virgin (in his note on Cosmas, Commentary on the Carmina of Gregory Nazianzen, Spicilegium Romanum vol. text: Dignum sane est, quod animadvertatur Sophronio quoque suffragante, non ex absoluta rei necessitate, sed ex decentia repetendum esse, quod Verbum Dei Filius, carnem humanam assumens, e matre Virgine præter naturæ ordinem nasci voluerit. Quæ quidem doctrina explorata adeo et scholæ theologis fuit, ut eximius Suarez (in part. III, q. 22, disp. 10, sect. 3), cum hanc thesim statuisset : Dicendum vero est, absque ulla dubitatione, potuisse Deum hominem concipi et generari ex muliere opera viri ; continuo subdat : Hanc assertionem censeo adeo certam, ut contraria nec probabilis nec verisimilis sit. Exinde vero liquet, haud rem acu eos tangere, qui putant, ideo ejusmodi conceptionis rationem in Christo repugnasse, quod repugnet, Christum originali Adæ peccato inflici potuisse, atque hinc permoveri se affirmant, ne Virginem Deiparam, quæ consueto naturæ ordine concepta est, ab Adamitico peccato exemptam fuisse existiment. Etiam si, inquit idem Suarez (in III part., quæst. 15, disp. 33, sect. 2), per seminalem propagationem conciperetur (Christus), si supponamus factam esse unionem a primo instanti conceptionis ejus, etiam non posset ex vi talis conceptionis peccatum originale contrahere. Curnam vero ? Quia scilicet non adeo necessarius est nexus inter generationem ab Adam ordinario modo deductam et originalem labem, ut hæc duo invicem sejungi, Deo sic dispensante, non queant. Hinc et illa nonnulorum Patrum sententia, sanctum Domini Præcursorem, quem nemo certe credidit sine seminali propagatione conceptum, ab originis vitio fuisse præservatum.
anchorLine: veniebat etiam, atque ipsi debebatur, (37) ut, remoto
en: It is worth noting that Sophronius too supports the view that the reason why the Word, the Son of God, taking human flesh, willed to be born of a Virgin mother beyond the order of nature is to be sought not in absolute necessity of the matter but in fittingness. This doctrine was so well explored even in the theologians' school that the eminent Suárez (part III, q. 22, disp. 10, sect. 3), having laid down the thesis 'It must be said, without any doubt, that God could have been conceived as man and generated of a woman by the act of a man,' at once adds: 'I judge this assertion so certain that the contrary is neither probable nor likely.' From this it is plain that those miss the point who think that such a manner of conception was repugnant in Christ because Christ could then have been tainted with Adam's original sin, and who say that they are moved by this so as not to suppose that the Virgin Mother of God, who was conceived in the customary order of nature, was exempt from Adamic sin. 'Even if,' says the same Suárez (part III, q. 15, disp. 33, sect. 2), 'Christ were conceived by seminal propagation, supposing the union made from the first instant of his conception, he still could not contract original sin by force of such a conception.' Why so? Because the link between generation derived from Adam in the ordinary way and the original stain is not so necessary that these two cannot be separated, God so ordaining. Hence also the opinion of some of the Fathers that the holy Forerunner of the Lord, whom surely no one believed to be conceived without seminal propagation, was preserved from the taint of origin.

en: Here is that doctrine, thoroughly explored among the holy Fathers: that it was fitting for the Mother to be as like the Son as possible. From this principle, while St. Sophronius here argues the Virgin's supreme humility and meekness, others, as we have seen, with equal right trace it back to the Virgin's purity and innocence, which is to be proclaimed free from any stain. See the oration of Isidore of Thessalonica, On the Nativity of the Mother of God, § 17, part 1, p. 243.

Manifeste hic Sophronius docet, hunc quoque errorem Nestorio tribuendum, quod Dominicæ carnis seu naturæ humanæ exsistentiam non contemporaneam qualicunque, quam admisit, conjunctioni cum Deo Verbo, sed plane huic præcedentem tradiderit. Et ne putes, his Samosatensem Paulum (qui § seq. simul cum Nestorio ac Theodoro memoratur) potius quam Nestorium impeti, vides quæ eadem de re Sophronius habet in celeberrima sua Synodica (supra) : Σαρκοῦται γοῦν Λόγος ὁ Θεός, ... οὐ προπλασθείσῃ σαρκὶ συναπτόμενος, ἢ προμορφωθέντι καὶ καθ᾽ αὑτὸ προϋποστάντι ποτὲ προσπλεκόμενος σώματι ... ἀλλὰ τότε τούτοις παραγενομένοις πρὸς ὕπαρξιν, ὅτε αὐτοῖς ὁ Λόγος ... συνετίθετο · φυσικῶς σύγχρονον ἔχοντα τῇ ὑπάρξει τὴν ἕνωσιν, καὶ οὐ πρὸ τῆς πρὸς τὸν Λόγον ἀληθεστάτης συμβάσεως καθ᾽ ἑαυτὰ γενόμενα πώποτε ... ἀλλὰ σύνδρομον ἔχοντα τῇ φυσικῇ τοῦ Λόγου συμβάσει τὴν ὕπαρξιν, καὶ οὐκ ἐκείνης, οὐδὲ ὡς ἐν ὀφθαλμοῦ ῥιπῇ ταύτην προτερεύουσαν ἔχοντα, ὡς Παῦλος ὁ Σαμοσατεὺς βομβεῖ καὶ Νεστόριος. Ἅμα γὰρ σάρξ, ἅμα Θεοῦ Λόγου σάρξ, κ. τ. λ. Incarnatur ergo Verbum Dei, ... non præformatæ carni semel coaptans, aut præformato corpori aliquando in se subsistenti se conjungens, sed his ad exsistentiam tunc venientibus, quando ipse Deus Verbum eisdem copulabatur : naturalem nempe unionem habent contemporaneam exsistentiæ, non vero exstiterunt in se aliquando ante verissimum cum Verbo conventum : ... sed synchronam naturali Verbi conjunctioni exsistentiam habent, non autem, ut Samosatensis Paulus ac Nestorius perstrepit, hanc illi tempore præcedentem habent, ne ictu quidem oculi. Simul quippe caro, simul Verbi Dei caro, etc.
Porro hæc quoque conferre debent ad abstergendam labem qua inconsulto vel sanctus pontifex Leo M. aspergitur. Scilicet cum Leo quoque et apertissime et sæpius (vid. epist. 59, ad cler. et pleb. Constantinop., cap. 5, epist. 102, ad episc. Galliar., cap. 3, et serm. 28, in Nativ. Dom., 8, cap. 5, edit. Baller.) Nestorium vitiati dogmatis circa tempus unionis Verbi cum carne incuset, jam si vera est sententia Joannis Garnerii (De hær. et libr. Nestor., diss. 1, § 3, pag. 286), de unionis tempore Nestorium ab Ecclesiæ sententia non recessisse, eo res adducitur, ut sanctus doctor insigni imprudentia (ne temeritate dicamus, aut calumnia) falsum Nestorio crimen dicendus sit imposuisse. Atqui hoc ipsum morari Garnerium debuit, ne præceps eam in opinionem veniret. Quid enim ? Nonne sanctus Leo quo tempore controversia Nestoriana agitabatur, sancti Cœlestini lateri, utpote Romanæ Ecclesiæ archidiaconus, assidebat, primasque in gerendis negotiis partes agebat ? Nonne sanctus Leo, [blotted: ?quod] Garnerius non diffitetur, ad manus habuit Nestorii scripta, etiam ea e quibus suam Garnerius opinionem firmat, quæ et refutanda ad Joannem Cassianum ante ipsam synodum Ephesinam transmisit ? Nonne, cum synodus Ephesina celebraretur, ad Leonem Cyrillus de gravissimis concilii negotiis, quo ad sanctum Cœlestinum deferrentur, scribebat ? Cuinam vero e Romano clero, vel quandonam apostolicæ sedi perspectas Nestorii res affirmabimus, si tunc incompertas putemus sancto Leoni, qui propterea tam crasse erraverit, atque insuper ad affirmanda ea, de quibus ignorabat, temere progressus fuerit ?
Miratur Garnerius (l. c.) hominum aliud Nestorio tribuentium sententiam. Atqui mirandum potius, quod tam facile sibi ipse suaserit, tot viros doctrina et sanctitate præclaros, quorum prolixum catalogum tum ex Oriente, tum ex Occidente, si locus ferret, facile foret subjicere, et quorum multi coævi factis fuerunt, nihil aut certe minus, quam ipse viderit, de hac re pervidisse, ac tenere scripsisse. Præsertim vero, quod summa argumentorum pro ea sententia in verbis demum Nestorii sita sit, ut merito domui in summa arena fundatæ comparari queat. Nunquid enim ea Nestorii dicta evincunt, ipsum aliter docuisse nunquam ? Sane ut id affirmes, unica tibi præsto est ratio, ut Nestorii in doctrinis semel prolatis constantiam vindices. Atqui occurret tibi sanctus Cœlestinus, quo auctore (Epist. ad Nestor., n. 2) Nestorius vera involvens obscuris, rursus utraque confundens, vel confitetur negata, vel nititur negare confessa ; occurret tibi et Marius Mercator, lectorem monens (Dissert. de XII anathem. Nest., n. 22), ut cautus sit de Nestorii varietate et inconstantia, quam, ait, utrum astutia an vecordia ad alliciendum auditorem habeat, non est facile nosse : quovis tamen pacto constat, eum varium esse, sibique contrarium. Agitur ergo de re judicata : ac tantumdem constantiæ Nestorii deferre licet, quantum fidei tribuere consuevimus hominis testimonio, qui solemni judicio maxime mendacissimus fuerit proclamatus. Non adeo ergo de ea constantia præsumendum fuit, ut tot Patres antiqui, quibus nemo unus e veteribus contradixerat, inscitiæ damnarentur.
Cæterum aliqua Garnerio excusatio ex eo non defuerit, quod Petavius, quem oppugnandum sibi proposuit, leviuscule hoc argumentum pertractaverat. Nunc autem eo minus dubitandi locus superest, quo certius corruunt et binæ ratiunculæ, quas Garnerius in rem suam addidit, scilicet 1. Quod Nestorius Mariam Χριστοτόκον constanter dixerit ; 2. anchorLine: lios et Christos dividere impiissime volentibus (42),
en:
Sophronius plainly teaches here that this error too is to be ascribed to Nestorius: that he handed down the existence of the Lord's flesh, or human nature, as not contemporaneous with whatever union with God the Word he admitted, but as plainly preceding it. And lest you think that Paul of Samosata (who is named with Nestorius and Theodore in the following section) rather than Nestorius is attacked here, see what Sophronius says on the same matter in his celebrated Synodica (above): 'The Word, God, is incarnate, ... not joined to flesh previously fashioned, nor interwoven with a body previously formed and ever self-subsisting ... but when these came into being, when the Word ... was composed with them: having the union naturally simultaneous with existence, and never having come into being by themselves before the truest conjunction with the Word ... but having their existence running together with the Word's natural conjunction, and not having it precede that, not even in the blink of an eye, as Paul of Samosata and Nestorius babble. For at once flesh, at once the flesh of God the Word,' etc. [Latin version:] 'The Word of God is incarnated, not joining himself once to flesh already formed, or to a body previously subsisting in itself, but these coming to existence at the moment God the Word was joined to them ... not, as Paul of Samosata and Nestorius shout, having this existence precede in time, not even by a moment. At once flesh, at once the flesh of the Word of God,' etc.
Moreover these things should also help wipe away the stain with which the holy pontiff Leo the Great is thoughtlessly spattered. For since Leo, too, both most openly and repeatedly (see letter 59, to the clergy and people of Constantinople, ch. 5; letter 102, to the bishops of Gaul, ch. 3; and sermon 28, on the Nativity of the Lord, 8, ch. 5, Ballerini ed.) accuses Nestorius of a corrupt doctrine about the time of the union of the Word with flesh, then, if Joannes Garnerius's view is true (On the heresies and books of Nestorius, diss. 1, § 3, p. 286) that Nestorius did not depart from the Church's view on the time of the union, matters come to this: that the holy doctor must be said, with remarkable imprudence (not to say rashness or calumny), to have imposed a false charge on Nestorius. Yet this very thing should have held Garnerius back from rushing into that opinion. For what? At the time the Nestorian controversy was in agitation, did not St. Leo, as archdeacon of the Roman Church, sit at St. Celestine's side and take the leading part in conducting business? Did not St. Leo, as Garnerius does not deny, have in hand the writings of Nestorius, even those from which Garnerius confirms his opinion, which he also sent to John Cassian to be refuted before the Council of Ephesus itself? Did not Cyril write to Leo, while the Council of Ephesus was being held, about the gravest business of the council, to be brought to St. Celestine? Whose affairs of Nestorius, then, among the Roman clergy, or when, shall we affirm to have been clearly known to the Apostolic See, if we suppose them unknown to St. Leo, who on that account erred so grossly and, further, rashly proceeded to affirm things of which he was ignorant?
Garnerius wonders at the opinion of men who attribute a different view to Nestorius. But rather it is wonderful that he so easily persuaded himself that so many men renowned for learning and holiness (whose long catalogue, East and West alike, it would be easy to append if space allowed, and many of whom were contemporaries) saw nothing in this matter, or at least less than he has seen, and wrote with understanding; especially since the sum of the arguments for that view rests only on Nestorius's words, so that it might justly be compared to a house built on the top of sand. Do those sayings of Nestorius prove that he never taught otherwise? To affirm that, the only ground you have is to vindicate Nestorius's constancy in the doctrines once set forth. But there will confront you St. Celestine, on whose authority (Letter to Nestorius, n. 2) Nestorius 'involving truths in obscurities, again confounding both, either confesses what he denied or strives to deny what he confessed'; and there will confront you Marius Mercator, warning the reader (Dissertation on the 12 anathemas of Nestorius, n. 22) to be 'wary of Nestorius's variability and inconstancy, which, he says, whether he has by craft or by madness to entice the hearer, is not easy to know: by any means, however, it is certain that he is changeable and self-contradictory.' The matter is therefore already judged: and we may grant to Nestorius's constancy only as much as we are wont to give of credence to the testimony of a man who has been proclaimed by solemn judgment most mendacious. It was therefore not so far to be presumed on that constancy that so many ancient Fathers, whom no one of the ancients had contradicted, should be condemned for ignorance.
Besides, some excuse for Garnerius may exist in that Petavius, whom he set himself to oppose, had handled this argument rather lightly. But now there is the less room for doubt, as the two little arguments Garnerius added for his own case collapse the more surely: namely 1. that Nestorius constantly called Mary Christotokos (Χριστοτόκος); 2. that Cyril did not reprehend such an error. For already since the year 1833 His Eminence Mai [published] St. Cy[ril] ... [note breaks off at foot of page; continues on the next page].

text: Cyrilli homiliam Græce edidit (Collect. vet. script., vol. VIII, part. II, pag. 108), eamque an. 1844 rursus dedit versione auctam (Nov. PP. Bibl., vol. II, pag. 75), qua utraque ea ratio plane eliditur. En tibi vel unam Cyrilli sententiam, qua et errorem illum arguit, et ideo abusive ab iis Mariam dici Christiparam contendit (n. 10, pag. 82) : Εἰ δὲ μετὰ τὴν ἕνωσιν χέχρισται, τὴν δὲ ἕνωσιν οὐ βούλονται λέγειν πρὶν ἐκ τῆς Παρθένου τεχθῆναι, οὐδὲ Χριστοτόκος οὐκέτι πρὸς αὐτῶν ἡ Παρθένος ὁμολογηθήσεται : Jam si post conjunctionem Jesus unctus fuit, conjunctionem autem nullam dicere volunt ante ejus ex Virgine ortum, sequitur ut isti ne Christiparam quidem Virginem fateantur. Et hæc quidem pauca pro argumenti, nimis forte multa pro loci ratione, ad tuendos Patres dicta fuerint.
en: ...Cyril's homily he published in Greek (Collectio vetera scriptorum [Collect. vet. script.], vol. VIII, part 2, p. 108), and in 1844 gave it again, enlarged with a version (Nova Patrum Bibliotheca [Nov. PP. Bibl.], vol. II, p. 75); by both, this reasoning is wholly dissolved. Here is even one sentence of Cyril by which he both convicts that error and contends that Mary is therefore called Christ-bearer (Christiparam) only abusively by them (n. 10, p. 82): 'But if he has been anointed after the union, and they do not wish to speak of the union before he was born of the Virgin, then not even Christotokos will any longer be confessed by them of the Virgin': 'Now if Jesus was anointed after the conjunction, and they are unwilling to speak of any conjunction before his birth of the Virgin, it follows that those men would not even confess the Virgin as Christ-bearer.' These things, indeed, are few for the argument, though perhaps too many for the place, to have been said in defence of the Fathers.

text: Communior apud Græcos inflexio nominis Manetis est Μάνης, Μάνους ; ita enim, ut aliquos allegem, Cyrillus Hierosol. (Catech. VI, n. 24), Nazianzenus (orat. 25, al. 23, § 8), Nyssenus (Contr. Eunomium, orat. 10), Chrysostomus (De Virginit., § 3), Epiphanius (hæres. 66, § 1, 2), Damascenus (De hæres., § 66). Eusebius tamen Cæsariensis (Hist. eccl. lib. VII, cap. 31) nomen pro Manetis ingenio flectens, utitur voce Μανέις, quasi a μαίνομαι (insanio) dictus sit, utpote qui, prout idem subdit, τὴν φύσιν μανιώδης (suapte natura furiosus) exstiterit, et τυφούμενος ἐπὶ τῇ μανίᾳ. Eadem de causa licet Socrates (Hist. eccl. lib. I, cap. 22) de Manete scripserit : μετονομάζει ἑαυτὸν Μάνην, (semel Manem appellat), tamen in titulo ejusdem capitis legimus : περὶ τοῦ Μανέντος. Utramque pariter formam habes in Historia Manichæorum a Petro Siculo conscripta, in qua (n. 41, apud Mai, N. PP. Bibl., tom. IV, part. II, pag. 15) et δυσώνυμος Μάντης (infausti nominis Manes) occurrit, et (n. 21, pag. 29) τοῦ Μανέντος μαθητὴς Κωνσταντῖνος (Manetis discipulus Constantinus), quanquam Petrus, non secus ac Socrates, scribit (n. 12, pag. 17) : ἀντὶ Κουβρίκου Μάνην ἑαυτὸν ὠνόμασεν (pro Cubrico Manetem se nominavit). Attamen Nicetas Choniates (de Manichæis, apud Mai, ibid., pag. 110) vocem Μανέντα adhibet, ubi et de nomine assumpto a Manete agit : Ἐκεῖνος γὰρ Κούβρικος ἐκαλεῖτο πρότερον, εἶτα μετεκάλεσεν ἑαυτὸν Μανέντα (Is enim antea Cubricus appellabatur ; deinde semet Manetem nominavit) ; licet nec alia forma desit apud eumdem Nicetam, qui mox subdit : Δηλοῖ δὲ ὁ Μάνης τῇ Βαβυλωνίων γλώσσῃ τὸ σκεῦος (significat autem Manes Babyloniorum lingua vas). Imo apud Theodoretum cernere est (Hæret. fabul. lib. I, c. 26) non modo Μάνης, et Μανέντος, sed tertia quadam inflexione εἰς Μάνητα. Hæc adnotata fuerint, ut pateat, quorsum Sophronius usus fuerit voce Μανέντες, quam eadem ætate usurpavit et sanctus Maximus, ubi (tom. II, p. 18) Severo exprobrat, quod et Μανέντος φαντασίαν docuerit.
anchorLine: ciones, Basilidæ, Manetesque (44) ac Mænandri,
en: A more common inflexion of the name of Manes among the Greeks is Μάνης, Μάνους; for so, to cite some, Cyril of Jerusalem (Catech. VI, n. 24), Nazianzen (orat. 25, al. 23, § 8), Nyssen (Against Eunomius, orat. 10), Chrysostom (On Virginity, § 3), Epiphanius (heresy 66, § 1, 2), Damascene (On Heresies, § 66). Eusebius of Caesarea, however (Eccl. Hist. book VII, ch. 31), bending the name to suit Manes's character, uses the form Μάνεις [as printed], as if he were so called from μαίνομαι (I am mad), inasmuch as, as he adds, he was 'by his very nature mad' and 'puffed up over his madness.' For the same cause, although Socrates (Eccl. Hist. book I, ch. 22) wrote of Manes 'he renames himself Manes' (he once calls himself Manes), yet in the title of that same chapter we read 'On Manentes' (περὶ τοῦ Μανέντος). You have both forms equally in the History of the Manichaeans composed by Peter of Sicily, in which (n. 41, in Mai, Nova Patrum Bibliotheca, vol. IV, part 2, p. 15) both 'ill-named Mantes' (Manes of ill-omened name) occurs, and (n. 21, p. 29) 'Constantine, disciple of Manes' (τοῦ Μανέντος μαθητής), although Peter, no differently from Socrates, writes (n. 12, p. 17): 'instead of Cubricus he named himself Manes' (pro Cubrico he named himself Manes). But Nicetas Choniates (On the Manichaeans, in Mai, ibid., p. 110) uses the form Μανέντα, where he also treats of the name assumed by Manes: 'For he was formerly called Cubricus, then renamed himself Manentas' (he was formerly called Cubricus; then named himself Manes); though another form is also found in the same Nicetas, who soon adds: 'Manes signifies in the language of the Babylonians a vessel' (Manes means in the language of the Babylonians a vase). Indeed in Theodoret (Fabulae haereticorum, book I, ch. 26) one sees not only Μάνης and Μανέντος, but by a third inflexion εἰς Μάνητα. Let this be noted so that it may be clear to what end Sophronius used the form Μανέντες, which Saint Maximus also used in the same age, where (vol. II, p. 18) he reproaches Severus that he also taught the 'phantasy of Manes' (Μανέντος φαντασίαν).

VI), non eadem tamen ratione oves suas pastor alloqui solebat.

en: And from these things it can be concluded that this oration was delivered by St. Sophronius while he was still living the monastic life, that is, before he undertook the governing of the Church of Jerusalem. For although a bishop dealing with a bishop sometimes calls himself 'the least' (ἐλάχιστον), as Cyrus of Alexandria in the inscription of his letter to Sergius of Constantinople (act. 13 of the Sixth Synod), yet a pastor was not accustomed to address his sheep in the same manner.

text: Eudoxius Arianus Constantinopolitanæ invasor sedis baptizavit Valentem imperatorem, cui se adjunxit Aetius magister Eunomii, dein ab Eudoxio constituti episcopi Cyziceni, quem expulsum apud se Constantinopoli detinuit. Ita Socr. l. IV, c. 1 et 7, et S. Epiphan. hæres. 75, n. 38, qui hæreticis Anomæis annumerat, quorum princeps Eunomius habebatur.
anchorLine: Abeant una cum his Eunomii et Eudoxii (10-11), et Asterii (12),
en: Eudoxius the Arian, usurper of the see of Constantinople, baptised the emperor Valens, to whom Aetius, the teacher of Eunomius, attached himself, and who was afterwards appointed bishop of Cyzicus by Eudoxius, who kept him with himself at Constantinople when he was expelled. So Socrates, book 4, chs. 1 and 7, and St. Epiphanius, heresy 75 [sic, as I read it], n. 38, who reckons him among the Anomoean heretics, whose leader Eunomius was held to be.
note: Combined double-number note (10-11), under NOTÆ, left column. Heresy number 75 read from the plate (Epiphanius' Anomoeans are 76; digit could be 73 or 75); Anchor line read from thumbnail.

text: Asterius Sophista in persecutione Maximiani Christianam fidem ejuravit. S. Epiphan. hæres. 76, n. 3. Agunt de eo homine Cappadoce et Ariano, ejusque libris Socr. l. I, c. 24 ; Sozom. l. II, c. 31 ; S. Athanasius De Synodo, aliique.
anchorLine: et Asterii (12), et cum ipsis Manichæi et Apollinarii (13),
en: Asterius the Sophist abjured the Christian faith in the persecution of Maximian. St. Epiphanius, heresy 76, n. 3. Socrates, book 1, ch. 24; Sozomen, book 2, ch. 31; St. Athanasius On the Synod, and others, treat of this man, a Cappadocian and an Arian, and of his books.

text: Apollinaris Laodiceni hæreses describit Epiphan. hæresi 77, n. 22 ; scilicet Christum corpus e cœlo detulisse, animam non assumpsisse, corpus divinitati consubstantiale fuisse. Agit de eo Sozomen. l. VI, c. 25, et alii : eum S. Damasus papa Romæ in synodo damnavit anno 373.
anchorLine: Manichæi et Apollinarii (13), Severi ac (14) Dioscori (15)
en: Epiphanius describes the heresies of Apollinaris of Laodicea in heresy 77, n. 22: namely that Christ brought a body from heaven, did not assume a soul, and that the body was consubstantial with the divinity. Sozomen, book 6, ch. 25, and others treat of him: Pope St. Damasus condemned him at Rome in a synod in the year 373.

text: Severus sedem Antiochenam expulso S. Flaviano per vim invasit anno 513, ex secta Acephalorum, oppugnator concil. Chalcedonensis. Coluntur SS. Flavianus, et Elias tunc quoque per ipsum e sede Hierosolymitana pulsus, 4 Julii.
anchorLine: Apollinarii (13), Severi ac (14) Dioscori (15),
en: Severus seized the see of Antioch by force in the year 513, St. Flavian having been expelled; he was of the sect of the Acephali and an opponent of the Council of Chalcedon. SS. Flavian, and Elias, who was likewise then driven from the see of Jerusalem by him, are honoured on 4 July.
note: Anchor word: the mark '(14)' follows 'ac' in 'Severi ac (14) Dioscori'. Anchor line read from thumbnail.

text: Dioscorus episcopus Alexandrinus patronus Eutychetis, cum eo in concilio Chalcedonensi damnatus. De eo agemus 18 Febr. ad Vitam S. Flaviani episcopi Constantinopolitani, ab ejus factionis hominibus in exsilium pulsi.
anchorLine: ac (14) Dioscori (15), omnisque Acephalorum (16)
en: Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria, patron of Eutyches, was condemned together with him at the Council of Chalcedon. We shall treat of him on 18 February, in the Life of St. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, who was driven into exile by men of his faction.
note: Spans left column foot into right column top ('Eutychetis, cum eo in concilio...'). Anchor line read from thumbnail.

text: Cum Petrus Moggus in sedem Alexandrinam anno 482 receptus, Henotico Zenonis imperatoris admisso, Catholicos simul et hæreticos offendisset, Eutychiani plures ab utrisque deficientes, Acephali, id est, sine capite sunt appellati : in varias mox sectas divisi.
anchorLine: omnisque Acephalorum (16) misera illa ac vere capite carens gangræna.
en: When Peter Mongus, received into the see of Alexandria in the year 482 on the admission of the emperor Zeno's Henoticon, had offended Catholics and heretics alike, many Eutychians, falling away from both sides, were called Acephali, that is, 'headless': they were soon divided into various sects.

text: Polemonem ex scriptis Apollinarii ansam nactum, dixisse in Christo substantiarum confusionem factam, et commistionem divinitatis et corporis tradit Theodoretus, l. IV Hæret. fabul. cap. 9.
anchorLine: et miseras Apollinarii Polemonisque (17) præstigias
en: Theodoret (Haereticarum fabularum book 4, ch. 9) reports that Polemon, having taken occasion from Apollinaris's writings, said that a confusion of substances was made in Christ, and a commingling of divinity and body.

text: Ebion princeps hæresis, quæ Christum nudum hominem appellavit, contra quem et Cerinthum S. Joannes suum Evangelium scripsit. Agunt de eo Theodoretus in compendio hæreticarum fabularum, earumque lib. II, cap. 1 ; S. Epiphanius hæresi 51, aliique.
anchorLine: Quibuscum Ebiones (18) ac Samosatenii (19)
en: Ebion, chief of the heresy which called Christ a mere man, against whom and against Cerinthus St. John wrote his Gospel. Theodoret treats of him in his compendium of heretical fables, book 2, ch. 1; St. Epiphanius, heresy 51, and others.

anchorLine: ac Samosatenii (19), Pauli et Bardesanæ
en: St. Ephrem the Syrian treats of Paul of Samosata in his Testament, in which, Theodoret reports (Haer. fab. book 1, ch. 22), Bardesanes is vigorously refuted; St. Epiphanius also treats of him, heresy 22.
